doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: Beginning liner notes: Prestige, Metronome and Jazz Journal
summary: Asked about liner notes, he describes the New York Post, Jazz Journal, Metronome and his first Prestige notes for Don Schlitten at $35.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Amazing. Now that’s a great AHA moment sort of. And I had them myself along the way here when the first couple of times some veteran musicians that I was interviewing would ask me about coming to the campus to play. In a sense they were trying to get a gig. And I remember thinking wow, this person here who’s had a long career, you make these assumptions like they must be doing great, they probably can stop working if they want. Definitely not the case. But I wanted to ask you about the writing of liner notes. What kind of parameters — first of all you’re hired by the record label usually?

Yeah. Usually — I mean my career as a liner notes writer began when my friend Don Schlitten, who was a noted producer, he was then with Prestige, and he asked me to do notes. See I went — after I got out of Brandeis I was at the New York Post, I was an editorial assistant in the so-called drama department, which was music, film and so on. I got to write one thing that was the first thing that was ever printed of mine actually, was a review of a Randall’s Island festival night in the New York Post. But then I eventually left there when I was offered the job at Metronome. That’s when I became a full-fledged jazz writer. Before that I had started writing for a British magazine, Jazz Journal. I wrote them a monthly news column. Anyway, Don asked me to do notes for a not particularly glamorous enterprise. It was an album by Willis Jackson, the tenor player, and it was called “Neapolitan Nights.” The program was all Italian-derived tunes, okay. So that was kind of neat to write about because I had to link this up with jazz and the history of that, you know “Come Back to Sorrento” by Vido Musso, you know. But that was the beginning. And Jesus, I couldn’t have made a living on this because Prestige at the time was paying 35 bucks for liner notes. This was in 1962. So it was a little more than it is now, and Prestige was one of the lower paying labels. So I did a bunch of stuff for Don, most of it of a more elevated, artistic nature than “Neapolitan Nights,” reissues, and — especially reissues. That became my first specialty sort of. And Don was doing a series of stuff — masters that they had leased from other labels. So that was the beginning, and then when “Metronome” folded very quickly I had the dubious distinction of being the last editor of “Metronome.” But it didn’t fold because of anything that we’d done wrong. Actually it was a very good magazine if I may say so. But the publisher had it as a tax write-off from his business. He had an electronic services company. This was 1961, in the relatively early days of things like computers and so on. So electronic servicing was a fairly new enterprise. And he was doing fairly well at it. But what happened then was that his biggest client, I forget who they were, said that either you become exclusively ours or we will take our business elsewhere.
